When they were released and sent home half a year later, they had already won a round against Quisling: they were still not members of his union, and his youth service had failed completely.

8:28 The net effect of the crackdown was to unite the whole country
Hansen's judgment was that Quisling's move against the teachers produced, as usual, the exact opposite of what he intended. Children, parents and teachers across the country were now united against him. One boy in his class joined the youth service — an organisation modelled on the German Hitler Youth — and was completely isolated and shunned by his classmates. In English lessons, the boy would trot out the startling claims from German propaganda about "British-Jewish-Marxist-plutocratic democracy," and could contribute nothing else. He also kept a notebook recording things Hansen had said that he considered offensive to his party or to Germans. Hansen said that sharing a classroom with this Quisling youth gave him a share of the Gestapo nightmare that had oppressed Europe since 1941.

9:35 The Germans won the land, not the schools
Norway was liberated on 8 May 1945; Quisling was subsequently arrested, sentenced to death, and shot by a firing squad in October 1945. A year before liberation, in his 1944 broadcast, Hansen looked back with pride on the resistance of himself and his colleagues and gave the sharpest line of the whole episode: the Germans conquered the whole of southern Norway in four weeks, but our schools fought another four-year war against the Germans, and we held our ground the whole time. The line splits military occupation and cultural resistance into two fronts, and explains why the teachers' noncooperation deserves to be remembered as a piece of history in its own right.

item.title: Home Depot Has the Best Return Since IPO, and It Isn't From Selling Cheap
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-acquired-home-depot-上市以来回报第一-靠的不是卖便宜货/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-acquired-home-depot-上市以来回报第一-靠的不是卖便宜货/
item.description: It packaged education into retail: a customer asks how to fix something, and the associate stops and teaches. A 25-cent washer leads to a $100,000 kitchen remodel — value that no Six Sigma spreadsheet can manage.
item.content:encoded:
It packaged education into retail: a customer asks how to fix something, and the associate stops and teaches. A 25-cent washer leads to a $100,000 kitchen remodel — value that no Six Sigma spreadsheet can manage.

A three-and-a-half-hour retail case study: the first half is 1970s financial engineering and startup gossip, the second half is a mechanism teardown of decentralization versus centralization and stock-based incentives. High information density.

1:08 North America only, yet worth more than Netflix
Home Depot has a $350 billion market cap, the 45th-largest public company in the world, worth more than Netflix, Alibaba, Goldman Sachs and LVMH. David stresses how crazy that is, because unlike those other companies it only does the North American market. Ben admits he had it wrong at first — he thought home improvement was just a big store in the middle of a shopping center, not a company that mattered to the world. The category is far bigger than he thought, and nearly all of its revenue comes from one continent.

2:16 Since its 1981 IPO, it's the S&P 500's top return
Home Depot went public in 1981, a year after Apple. If you had put $1,000 into each and held to today, Home Depot's return would beat Apple's; with dividends reinvested, that's roughly 25% compounded annually over 45 years. It is the single best-performing stock in the S&P 500 from its listing date to today: $1,000 would become about $17 million, versus just $170,000 for the S&P 500 over the same period. David notes that who holds this equity is itself a key part of the company's strategy — early employee ownership and long-term share price growth are the same mechanism.

42:12 Home Depot is not a Price Club clone
What Bernie set out to build was not a low-SKU warehouse club but a warehouse where you buy everything for one job: Price Club carried only 4,000 SKUs, while Home Depot would stock 25,000 and deal with a huge number of suppliers. Gross margin was set below the industry too — hardware retail's standard at the time was 45%, and they ran at 30%. Another fundamental difference was the nature of the goods: anyone will buy toilet paper, but nobody is born knowing how to build a deck, hang blinds or lay flooring, so the store had to be staffed with a knowledgeable workforce — and Price Club's org structure was never designed for that.

1:26:09 Big-box stores aren't the moat; service is
In the 1980s a pile of capital rushed into the category: Builders Square, Home Club, Home Quarters Warehouse, Mr. HOW Warehouse, all copying Home Depot, and today not one of them is left. David's explanation: Home Depot is not "Costco for hardware." Costco is general-merchandise retail, where customers need no human help beyond the checkout lane; Home Depot is specialty retail, where price, selection and convenience — the "trinity" — aren't enough, and you also have to provide something unique to the category, the way a tire shop has to mount tires, a beauty store has to let you try makeup, and Apple has to have a Genius Bar. Home Depot essentially invented "serving the customer" in the home improvement category itself.

1:35:12 Low margin rides on turnover, not margin rate
Home Depot's warehouse model has two structural disadvantages: an extremely high SKU count and an extremely large in-store service staff, which makes fast turnover operationally hard, and per-store labor costs higher than the price club model. Ben says what holds it all up is "manufacturing buying frenzy" — with that many SKUs, you have to give people a reason to buy across all of them. The key line: what feeds the company is not the gross margin percentage but gross margin dollars. So it needs enough volume and fast enough turnover that the gross margin dollars add up to justify the store carrying all that inventory. Once volume is there, it can place bigger orders with suppliers, demand lower prices, and pass the savings to customers, spinning the whole wheel faster.

1:53:38 It invented the national chain, so no one could buy nationally
Home Depot's early philosophy was radical decentralization, letting stores use local knowledge to decide what to stock and how much; Bernie estimated this made per-store sales 15% to 20% higher. But at scale, the costs of decentralization outweighed the benefits: operational chaos, systems and technology that couldn't be unified, and countless decision-makers and negotiators facing the same suppliers without getting the best prices. Ben makes a key point: this problem didn't exist for anyone else, because the very concept of a "national hardware chain" was invented by Home Depot — before it, nobody bought nationally, so there was no national purchasing opportunity to have.

2:12:04 Replacing knowledgeable staff with 16-year-old cashiers
Nardelli replaced a large share of store associates with part-time general-retail labor, effectively killing the whole philosophy of "a knowledgeable person sells you a 25-cent washer, fixes your sink, and brings in the big follow-on order." According to Arvind's research, from 2000 to 2006 store staff fell from 200 to 170, a 15% cut. Store manager standards changed too, with a preference for college-educated candidates — while the associates hired in the stores had no college degrees, effectively telling those people they were locked into jobs with no promotion path. The result: customer satisfaction fell to the lowest among major U.S. retailers, while revenue and profit doubled.

2:20:10 Pay not tied to the stock price means no value stored in the company
Ben nails the incentive misalignment: if pay is tied to the stock price, you don't care about current-period results — you want investors to believe you're storing long-term value in the company, so you keep prices low, push volume, and make customers fanatical; if pay is tied to today's numbers, you don't store value in the company, you just pump today's numbers. David calls it "the paradoxical misalignment of incentives." Nardelli refused to tie any compensation to the stock price, on the grounds that the stock price was the one metric he couldn't control — which cut directly against the core of the company model: the associate's promise had always been "I do good work, the stock goes up, I get rich."

item.title: Dennett Denies Qualia: Color Is Neither Out There Nor In Here
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-pel-丹尼特否认感受质-颜色不在外面-也不在里面/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-pel-丹尼特否认感受质-颜色不在外面-也不在里面/
item.description: Dennett doesn't deny that we seem to have qualia; he denies that qualia, as a reified thing, exist — just as the center of gravity is an abstraction, not a point in the body.
item.content:encoded:
Dennett doesn't deny that we seem to have qualia; he denies that qualia, as a reified thing, exist — just as the center of gravity is an abstraction, not a point in the body.

Four hosts read and argue their way through qualia, the self, and the bat argument in chapters 12 to 14 of Consciousness Explained. Medium information density, suited to anyone trying to pin down what exactly Dennett is denying.

5:00 Consciousness comes in degrees, not all or nothing
Dennett would say consciousness is a matter of degree: a thermostat is "aware" of temperature at the lowest degree, because it registers temperature. Cockroaches and Venus flytraps count too. The key mechanism is self-looping and self-stimulation — a bunch of clumsy little homunculi each making distinctions, and stacked together they add up to full consciousness. For Dennett, as long as information is globally available to the organism, that is consciousness in the full sense. Block would counter: that's only access consciousness, you still need the "lights coming on" part. Host Dylan protests on the spot: we haven't even read Block, don't rope us in with that name.

7:00 Qualia are a relic of the Cartesian theater
Seth recounts Dennett's genealogy: primary qualities (size, shape, motion, number) can be attributed to objects in the world; secondary qualities (color and the like) end up lodged in the subject's subjective experience. Dennett's key move is to tie secondary qualities to the Cartesian theater — once you say color isn't out there and can only be in here, you've presupposed an "in here" theater where experience is presented to someone. That is exactly what he wants to tear down.

12:52 He doesn't deny the seeming, only the being
On page 372 Dennett lines up raw feels, sensa, phenomenal qualities, intrinsic properties of conscious experience and a pile of other terms, and says he doesn't care about the fine distinctions between any of them. He denies that these properties exist, but fully agrees that "there seem to be qualia" — because science does seem to prove that color can't be out there, so it can only be stuffed in here. Dylan sums it up: this is precisely the inference Dennett wants to dismantle.

15:02 A color robot doesn't need a screen
On pages 373 to 375 Dennett compares color: you can look at things in the world side by side, or you can just recall or imagine them in your mind. Mark throws out the term: a color-discriminating robot has access consciousness, it can use information to make distinctions, but we intuitively feel that isn't enough, that qualia are still needed. Dylan pushes back: you still haven't told me what exactly is missing. He demands an example that doesn't involve discrimination, comparative memory, the mind's eye, or linguistic communication. Christopher says color is a bad example; better ones are mental fatigue, valence states, pain.

26:50 The self is a center of gravity, not an observer
Seth describes Dennett's analogy as "the law of universal gravitation"; Dylan corrects him: it's the center of gravity. The center of gravity is an abstracted, centralized organizing principle that explains what happens around an object, but the closer you get to that center the more it breaks down. Dylan says this is exactly what he finds persuasive: the failure of measurement matches "we don't have continuous experience, only chopped-up discrete experience stitched back together." Drill down and you won't find consciousness at every level; consciousness emerges from the assembly.

31:01 The self isn't a judge, it's the activity itself
Dylan says Dennett doesn't deny you have a self, he denies that the self is the witness sitting above all experience passing judgment. The self is the assembly of this pile of stuff. Christopher adds a better word: the self is an activity. Dylan picks it up: that's why it's so tightly bound to the narrative model — the self is the event of these distinctions and discriminations continuously happening at this location, on this entity. Dennett uses multiple personality, divided selves, and split brains — these "natural bad experiments" — to argue that the self is a kind of unity, and that this is consistent with the multiple drafts model.

39:00 Qualia can't live only inside an illusion
Seth runs a live experiment: he has everyone look at the device with the cord on the table behind Dylan and asks what color it is; everyone says blue. He asks: did you pull up a blue from memory to compare against? No. Dylan rebuts the experiment: when we're uncertain we say "it looks blue to me," and that's a qualifier, used in situations where you might be deceiving me or I might be having an optical illusion. Seth says that isn't his point: qualia can't exist only in epistemically uncertain hypothetical cases, and that shared, uncontroversial blue experience just now already can't be adequately captured in the language of scientific materialism.

45:40 Bats are as inaccessible as a Leipzig audience
Dennett reinterprets the bat through the Leipzig example: imagine what it was like to hear a Bach cantata for the first time — you'd have to reconstruct the context, history, environment, religious state, do a huge amount of work to get as close as you can. Seth says this is a good example, because even a fifteenth- or sixteenth-century human of the same species can't get in, let alone a bat. Dylan cites page 442: what we should care about is what we can know about the bat's consciousness (if it has one), not whether we can temporarily or permanently turn our mind into a bat's mind. Mark points out that qualia lovers will seize on exactly this: bats have echolocation, you don't, so you'll never know what it's like.

item.title: A Soviet Spy's Embarrassing Secret Nearly Stopped World War III
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-historyhit-一个苏联间谍的难言之隐-差点阻止了第三次世界大战/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-historyhit-一个苏联间谍的难言之隐-差点阻止了第三次世界大战/
item.description: In 1981, a senior KGB officer in Tehran walked into MI6 and volunteered — not for money or ideology, but because he believed the West could cure his erectile dysfunction. The intelligence he handed over led the US and Britain to give the Soviets' coup plan to the Iranians.
item.content:encoded:
In 1981, a senior KGB officer in Tehran walked into MI6 and volunteered — not for money or ideology, but because he believed the West could cure his erectile dysfunction. The intelligence he handed over led the US and Britain to give the Soviets' coup plan to the Iranians.

Ben Macintyre tells a Cold War spy story that has never been told, with astonishing detail and tight pacing — though the information density is concentrated in the second half, on the coup and its aftermath, while the setup runs a little long.

0:00 A spy story that has never been told
Ben Macintyre's new book Redwood tells a Cold War story that had never been made public before: in 1981, a senior KGB officer in Tehran, Vladimir Kuzichkin, walked into MI6 and volunteered, becoming a double agent codenamed "Redwood." The intelligence he provided revealed that the Soviets were plotting a coup through the Iranian communist Tudeh Party to overthrow Khomeini's government, after which the Red Army would cross into Iran from Afghanistan, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan. The Pentagon's answer to that was nuclear strike — because conventional forces were not enough to stop a full Soviet invasion. What makes the story so strange is that Kuzichkin's motive for defecting was intensely personal: he suffered from erectile dysfunction and believed Western medicine could cure him.

3:01 1981 came closer to nuclear war than the Cuban Missile Crisis
Macintyre points out that 1981 was one of the closest moments of nuclear confrontation in the Cold War, second only to the Cuban Missile Crisis. After the Iranian Revolution, every faction — nationalists, liberals, communists and Islamists — was fighting for power, and Tehran became a "seething cauldron of spies." The CIA, MI6 and the KGB all poured in at once. The Soviets had just invaded Afghanistan and were doing well, while the Americans were desperate to re-establish a foothold in the Middle East. If the Soviets took Iran, they could control the warm-water ports and the oil fields and win the Cold War. So the Pentagon was already drawing up nuclear options, including using portable nuclear weapons to blow up mountain ranges and block Soviet armored columns.

8:18 The CIA was blind in Tehran; MI6 kept a man there illegally
After the Iran hostage crisis, the CIA was thrown out of Tehran, had no human intelligence in Iran at all, and knew nothing about a possible Soviet coup. The only service still capable of operating was MI6, but Britain's condition for maintaining a diplomatic mission in 1981 was "no spying of any kind." MI6 nevertheless sent Ian McCready in under commercial counselor cover — a huge gamble by the British government. McCready's instructions were "do nothing, recruit no one, keep a low profile" — because if he was caught, the Iranians would take the entire embassy hostage. He could only communicate with London using a World War II-era cipher machine called RockX, an extremely cumbersome device of which only two existed in the world.

12:29 His motive was impotence, not money or ideology
Kuzichkin was a senior officer at the KGB residency in Tehran, in charge of illegal spy programs across the entire Middle East, and the only defector who understood how the illegal system worked. He walked into MI6 and offered to spy for the West. The spy world has an acronym, MICE — money, ideology, coercion, ego — but Kuzichkin fit none of the categories. He was partly alienated from the regime, but the root cause was this: he suffered from erectile dysfunction and believed the West had a drug that could cure it. He had just married, loved his wife deeply, and could not reveal the secret to his KGB colleagues or to a Soviet doctor. McCready did not mock him or exploit him; he took him with extreme seriousness, even sending MI6 headquarters an unprecedented telex: "Help. What do I do with a spy who has erectile dysfunction?"

21:52 He photographed every KGB file in the Middle East
For nearly a year, McCready ran Kuzichkin by old-fashioned means: dead drops, brush contacts, a miniature camera. He gave Kuzichkin a Minox camera to carry into the office every day and photograph every document he could get his hands on. In the end the Redwood archive filled four truckloads. MI6 gave him the codename "Redwood" — because he was six foot four, and because they could not resist the pun: Red for communism, Wood for his "problem." Kuzichkin's core intelligence was this: the Soviets were plotting a coup through the Tudeh Party, the money and weapons were already in place, the Tudeh had a secret military underground, and Kuzichkin himself was the coordinator between the KGB and the Tudeh.

29:05 The US and Britain handed the coup plan to the Iranians
After Kuzichkin fled to Britain, MI6 debated internally whether to use the intelligence. Chris Cohn, who ran the operations directorate and later became chief of MI6, argued it had to be used. If they did not use it, he said, intelligence about a Tudeh communist coup was meaningless. So MI6 sent Redwood to Islamabad, Pakistan, under diplomatic cover, to meet Iranian intelligence. The meeting lasted three days, Kuzichkin laid everything out, and MI6 handed the Iranians all four truckloads of intelligence. It was also an attempt to open a secret channel to Iran at a moment when relations with the West were at rock bottom. It was deeply illegal, and if it had come out it would have been a huge scandal — the British and American governments acting to protect the Islamic Revolution.

31:05 Iran used the intelligence to execute eight thousand communists
Once the Revolutionary Guard had the intelligence, within two months it arrested eight thousand Iranian communists, about half of whom were executed. This became a cornerstone of Iran's modern theocratic state. From that moment on, Khomeini tolerated no opposition at all; everyone was purged, including people already in prison, and it turned into a massacre. It also hardened two convictions of the Islamic Revolution: first, that all opposition must be destroyed, because fifth columns were everywhere; second, that whatever happens, the British are behind it. MI6 and the CIA inadvertently consolidated the Iranian regime and created a monster — almost an exact replay of Afghanistan, where money poured in to Islamic guerrillas fighting the Soviets and ultimately produced al-Qaeda, ISIS and 9/11.

38:11 History is often driven by perception, not fact
Macintyre stresses that it is impossible to know whether the Soviets would actually have carried out the coup, but everyone involved believed they would. McCready believed it, Kuzichkin believed it, and MI6, the CIA, the KGB and the Tudeh themselves all believed it. That was enough — nuclear war can break out on the basis of perception rather than fact, and the same was true of the Cuban Missile Crisis. Would Khrushchev really have used those weapons? We do not know, but everyone believed he might. The story was never told because none of the participants wanted it told: not the Iranians, because it meant the West had outsmarted them again; not the KGB, because it was a humiliation — they had failed to spot the defector, 18 Soviet diplomats were expelled from Iran as a result, the entire Tudeh operation was dismantled, and agent networks across the Middle East and even in Canada were exposed.

item.title: After You Die, What's Left Isn't the Cause of Death — It's the You That Others Assemble
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-tal-死后你留下的不是死因-是别人拼凑的你/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-tal-死后你留下的不是死因-是别人拼凑的你/
item.description: All three stories do the same thing: once a person is dead, friends and family can only reconstruct someone who can no longer speak from fragments — texts, obituaries, Facebook comments — and the version they piece together often doesn't match how the person saw themselves at all.
item.content:encoded:
All three stories do the same thing: once a person is dead, friends and family can only reconstruct someone who can no longer speak from fragments — texts, obituaries, Facebook comments — and the version they piece together often doesn't match how the person saw themselves at all.

A narrative show, no data or mechanisms, but each of the three stories has a twist, and the second story's twist is the most valuable. Medium information density, good for the commute.

5:12 After you die, people will get you wrong
As a kid, Graham was playing on a seesaw at a construction site and dropped a 25-pound curbstone from second-story height, trying to launch a brick off the other end. The brick didn't fly — it shot straight at his face and grazed past his hair. He survived, but decades later what he keeps thinking about isn't the terror of that second, it's something else: if the brick had actually killed him, how would a coroner have read the scene? A brick, a seesaw, a child — could they have pieced together the truth? This is where the show states the premise of the whole episode — death itself isn't the hardest part; the hard part is the judgment others make about who you were after you're gone.

12:15 She has now outlived her sister
Nadia wrote a long letter to the drug dealer who killed her sister. The sharpest cut in it isn't anger, it's arithmetic: at 6:49 p.m. on March 11, 2018, she outlived her sister's age — she had been in the world a few seconds longer than the sister who was two and a half years older. She says it makes no sense, that he bent the universe. She went through her sister's phone, read the texts, listened to the voicemails, trying to figure out the life her sister had finally refused to share with her. She even admits she needs this dealer: because of him she can say "if it weren't for that person," and she doesn't have to hate her sister, or hate herself.

20:28 The message she never answered became the last one
A few days before her sister died, her sister sent a trivial text asking if she remembered the little illustrated figure named faible (weak) in their middle-school French textbook. It was an old joke between the sisters. Nadia was still angry about their last fight and deliberately didn't reply, wanting to punish her a little. But a strong thought surfaced: you don't want this to be the last message she ever sends you. She still didn't reply. After her sister died, she found a text her sister had sent a friend that night: "How do I stop hating my sister? My family really hates me." The friend replied: "Damn, Nadia the snitch." When she saw the word "hate" next to her own name, she was hollowed out.

33:53 He lived to read his own eulogies
Comedian Dave Marr was in a diabetic coma for a month; his friends thought he was going to be taken off the tube, more than fifty people gathered at his house for a vigil, and 1,700 Facebook friends started writing eulogies on his wall. Then his parents didn't pull the tube, he was transferred, and he woke up. After recovering, he sat in his parents' basement from 2 a.m. to 3:30 a.m. and read through about a hundred eulogies. He read that his brother's post trying to set the record straight got buried by the algorithm with only 70 likes, while the posts mourning him got double that. He read someone remembering how he'd bashed in a storage-room door at a party insisting it was the bathroom, read an ex-girlfriend thanking him for breaking up with her in the car because it was cold outside, read someone saying he "sweats unreasonably much."

42:06 The man in the eulogies he doesn't recognize
After reading all the eulogies, Dave wasn't moved — he felt bad. The self he remembered was someone who shoplifted at Walgreens and spent a night in jail; the self in the eulogies was known by every Walgreens clerk, bought people free Chipotle, treated everyone as an equal. He says it's hard to square the image in his own head with the image people described when they thought he was dead. He insists the coma was his own doing — "it was my carelessness, my recklessness that got me here." And Blake's side is a different story: he lost a friend and got him back, and now Dave's laugh is like music to him. The show says both men got a second chance, to love and to be loved, and the latter is much harder than the former.

57:33 Nobody mentioned how he died
Charlie, a retired Navy officer, went in a friend's place to the funeral of a SEAL he'd never met, Eddie Furlani. He couldn't find any reporting on the cause of death and assumed it was a training accident. At the funeral he noticed the back rows full of big men in three-piece suits and sunglasses, expressionless the whole time, until Eddie's seven-year-old daughter Zelma broke down crying and was taken out by her stepmother. After the service he called his friend to report back, and the friend said, "I'm glad someone came, I was worried no one would," then added, "because of the way he killed himself." Charlie says that moment was like grabbing a live wire — no reporting, no mention in the obituary, not a word in the eulogy.

59:47 The daughter cried because she felt ashamed
The day before the interview, Charlie called Eddie's widow to confirm, and only then learned that Zelma had cried and asked to leave the funeral not out of grief but out of shame — she thought everyone knew her dad had killed himself, and that she was a bad person. Charlie says hearing this terrified him: a seven-year-old girl treating herself as an outcast because of her father's death, when the room was full of people who had come to support her. He also talks about veterans losing their "larger mission" after they leave the service, and says he can probably put himself in Eddie's shoes and understand what he was thinking in that moment, but when asked whether he could say more, he stops and says he can't take on that subject.

1:02:00 He wanted to be the sound of that helicopter
Charlie has had suicidal thoughts himself; this ended his Navy career, and he only agreed to talk about it after the mic was off. The host asks whether he wrote the piece because Eddie's funeral could be his own future funeral, and he says no. He explains the real reason: on medevac flights he knew that the sound of the helicopter approaching alone could improve a dying person's vitals. He says, I'm writing to you because I want to be that helicopter's sound for someone. The show ends with the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, 800-273-TALK.

item.title: The British Expedition to Abyssinia: An Emperor Seizes Every Diplomat
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-restishistory-英国远征阿比西尼亚-一个皇帝把外交官全扣了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-restishistory-英国远征阿比西尼亚-一个皇帝把外交官全扣了/
item.description: Victoria never answered one letter, so Tewodros II locked the British consul and a batch of missionaries inside Magdala at the top of a mountain — and got an expeditionary force in return.
item.content:encoded:
Victoria never answered one letter, so Tewodros II locked the British consul and a batch of missionaries inside Magdala at the top of a mountain — and got an expeditionary force in return.

The first half is a long build, but the second half has an extremely high density of detail on the hostage crisis and the emperor's psychological collapse — suited to listeners interested in imperial history and negotiation games.

0:00 One unanswered letter lit the war
Tewodros II wrote a letter to Queen Victoria, phrased like a pen pal: ‘How are you? I am well, thank God.’ The letter travelled by way of the Red Sea, Aden, Bombay, Suez, Alexandria, Marseille and London, halfway around the world, and ended up filed by the Foreign Office in the India Office records. No one replied. The emperor waited two years, his expectation turning to suspicion, and concluded that Britain was colluding with his Muslim enemies. In 1864 he seized the British consul Cameron and a group of missionaries, and the hostage crisis began.

10:21 He claimed descent from Solomon, and meant it
Abyssinia had a legend: a descendant of Solomon and David would rise, unify the divided kingdom, defeat the Egyptians, and march all the way to Jerusalem, and his name would be Tewodros. In 1855 Kassa, a man of obscure origins who had been a bandit chief, defeated his last rival and proclaimed himself the new emperor, taking the name Tewodros II. He later claimed to be of Solomon's line, though he said nothing of it when Plowden first met him. This messianic identity was both the source of his legitimacy and the root of his later paranoia.

21:46 After his wife died he began to lose control
In 1858 Tewodros's wife Tewabech died, and he was grief-stricken. His next wife, the 12-year-old Tiruwork, was cold to him and said, ‘I am speaking with a king greater than you — get out.’ He began drinking heavily, sleeping with women in the camp at random, and admitted to the missionaries that he was living ‘a very unchristian and indecent life.’ In 1860 his friend Plowden was ambushed by rebels and died nine days after taking a spear wound. Britain sent a new representative only two years later, and in the interval the emperor's paranoia deteriorated sharply.

26:55 The letter Cameron carried back became the fuse
At the end of 1862, when Cameron left the emperor's camp, he took with him a letter in which Tewodros asked Victoria to arrange safe passage for his envoy, and said, ‘See how Islam oppresses the Christians.’ Cameron returned saying he had received no reply from London, and the emperor began to suspect he had gone off to Sudan to collude with the Muslims. In October 1863 the missionary Stern angered the emperor by publishing his book Wanderings among the Falashas, and was arrested, whipped and put in chains. In January 1864 Cameron and the other missionaries were also seized, and all the hostages realised the nightmare had only just begun.

39:33 What Britain really feared was France
The Foreign Office did not particularly care whether the missionaries lived or died; what worried them was France. Suez Canal fever was at its height, and if they alienated Tewodros he might turn to Paris, and France could then control the route from the Red Sea to India. So they sent Hormuzd Rassam — Mosul-born Assyrian, archaeologist, discoverer of Ashurbanipal's palace and the Epic of Gilgamesh, Oxford-educated, a convert to Protestantism, and fervently pro-British. He set out for Abyssinia with a letter from Queen Victoria and two assistants, Dr Blanc and Lieutenant Prideaux.

49:02 Rassam nearly succeeded, then was seized himself
In January 1866 Rassam, in his blue diplomatic uniform, met Tewodros, and after reading Victoria's letter the emperor was so excited he could not sleep; the next day he dictated a reply calling the queen ‘the defender of religion chosen by God.’ He agreed to release all the hostages, but demanded that Rassam first accompany him on a campaign to put down rebels. Along the way the emperor kept sending gifts: muskets, manuscripts, salmon, antelope, two lion cubs, two monkeys and a baboon. In March 1866 the hostages were finally brought to the lake, but on 13 April, when Rassam went to say goodbye, he found that he too had been arrested.

57:19 He held everyone just to get gunmakers
Why did Tewodros seize Rassam? There are three possibilities: he had been acting all along; he was overcome at the last moment by his hatred of the missionaries; or he genuinely liked Rassam and could not bear to let him go. Philip Marsden thinks the third most likely — the emperor was infatuated with Rassam and saw him as his only channel to British friendship and British technology. The emperor then wrote to Victoria demanding that she send ‘skilled craftsmen, blacksmiths, gunsmiths, artillery experts’ to make guns, and said he would release the prisoners once he was satisfied.

1:02:28 In the cellar he admitted he was mad
Tewodros locked the missionaries in a cellar, came in with a bottle of arak, and sat down among them drinking and talking. At last he said, calmly and sadly: ‘My father was mad. People often said I was mad, and I never believed them. But now I know it is true.’ Rassam urged him not to say such things; the emperor walked to the door, turned back, and in a hoarse whisper said: ‘I am mad. Goodbye.’ Then he left. For nearly two years afterwards they were held on the mountain-top of Magdala, at ten thousand feet, in chains, their spines bent.

item.title: Compute goes from shortage to glut in 2027, and the AI bubble may not pop
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-asianometry-2027-年算力会从短缺变成过剩-ai-泡沫未必破/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-asianometry-2027-年算力会从短缺变成过剩-ai-泡沫未必破/
item.description: Usable AI data center capacity is about 15 gigawatts at the end of 2026 and races to 45-55 gigawatts by the end of 2027, a 30-40 gigawatt increment. At $50 billion of revenue per gigawatt, the two giants would have to produce $750 billion to $1.5 trillion, and that number does not hold up.
item.content:encoded:
Usable AI data center capacity is about 15 gigawatts at the end of 2026 and races to 45-55 gigawatts by the end of 2027, a 30-40 gigawatt increment. At $50 billion of revenue per gigawatt, the two giants would have to produce $750 billion to $1.5 trillion, and that number does not hold up.

The first half is on-the-ground observation from Hot Chips and Semicon Taiwan; the second half is the real value of this episode: a bottom-up arithmetic of compute supply and demand, plus the judgment that anti-AI sentiment could swing elections.

3:05 The window for new AI chips has reopened
Last year the author wrote that ‘the window for new AI chips has closed, except for Google's TPU’, and here he explicitly takes it back and says he was wrong. The trigger was OpenAI unveiling its in-house chip Jalapeno at Hot Chips, a short talk with high information density. Outside the hall a ring of new AI chip startups was gathered: Etched, MatX, Posetron, Fractile. Etched gave no talk but built presence by handing out hats while its founder roamed the Q&A asking questions. The author cautions that these are hardware companies: they do not just design chips, they have to build their own racks and systems and work in the lab, and recruiting top talent and execution are hard bars. His survival test borrows Nathan Bedford Forrest's controversial line: get there first, and with the most men.

6:08 Semicon Taiwan is really TSMC's request for proposal
First-timers are surprised: neither TSMC nor ASML has a booth. But TSMC dominates the whole show — its teams walk the halls visiting new suppliers and scouting new technology, and many information sessions have TSMC executives on stage laying the company's problems out in public. The author's conclusion is that Semicon Taiwan is essentially an RFP that TSMC issues to the entire semiconductor industry. The technical throughline is clear: future manufacturing has to go big. AI chips are hitting existing limits, most typically the reticle limit, which determines how large an area a lithography machine can print. TSMC had a slide showing it is preparing to build a ‘battleship-class’ chip spanning 14 reticles, and the industry responds fast, as always.

7:10 Glass panel packaging has gone from PPT to the show floor
Two years ago the author made a video on panel level packaging, which was the theme of Semicon Taiwan 2024, when it was still all talks and slideshows. Now AI systems are so large that the industry wants to use square, glass panel interposers to carry chiplets and memory instead of silicon interposers. The author's attitude is reserved: can TSMC make them without warping or cracking? ‘I'll believe it when I see the chip.’ But the ecosystem is already moving, and equipment such as handling robots adapted to square panels has appeared on the show floor. He judges this wave of ‘chipmaxing’ will be one of the most far-reaching technology transitions in semiconductor history, roughly on the scale of the move to 300-millimeter wafers.

8:12 The spot market has vanished, and VCs now help portfolio companies find GPUs
When the author was last in the Bay Area in September 2025, the picture was completely different. Since then long-running agentic AI has swept Silicon Valley, triggered in part by stronger models such as Anthropic's Opus 4.5 around November 2025 and by Open Claw. In February 2026 prices began to rise, everyone scrambled to lock up compute, and Anthropic led the way signing big deals with SpaceX, Google and others. The author was told that by the time of this trip the spot market had completely vanished. For Neoclouds (a term coined by semi-analyst Dan Nishbal in April 2024 for pure cloud vendors that resell AI training and inference compute, such as Coreweave and Nebius) this is a huge boon, and they are confident the shortage will last at least another one to two years. The author met several people who did not know each other and each wanted to start a Neocloud. For AI startups this is a business risk: imagine telling investors your product has to wait until mid-2027 because there is not enough compute. The new way VCs help portfolio companies is to go find compute, and he heard of people scraping together a thousand GPUs and hunting in unexpected places as far off as Eastern Europe.

9:12 Two giants are feasting while compute still goes to waste
By contrast, Anthropic and OpenAI are feasting internally. Dylan recently said on Dashpod that these two AI giants each have about 5 gigawatts of compute. The author infers from this that a considerable share of all that compute may be wasted, and anecdotes he heard confirm that this ‘filthy rich’ state is not being used as efficiently as it could be. He also asked every AI insider he talked to one question: will Google return to the frontier? The general consensus is no, though the explanations are vague. Several people pointed out that Google's decision to sell a large amount of compute to Anthropic is itself a sign that it does not believe. This is a big reversal from the period when Gemini 3 made some people think OpenAI was finished. What the author heard is that Google suffered severe talent drain, plus a culture unfriendly to frontier AI.

11:15 Neolabs are venture capital that treats compute as money
What fascinates the author most is the Neolab: a research startup with basically no revenue that raises money to explore an interesting AI idea, whose founders are often elite researchers and whose business plan is little more than ‘discover an entirely new architecture’. The most famous and earliest, Safe Superintelligence, raised a billion dollars and has still released no product or model. The label is fuzzy and covers recursive intelligence, Humans, Core Automation, Flapping Airplanes and others; those with products include Japan's Sakana AI, Thinking Machines, Reflection AI, plus a batch in verticals such as materials science, world models and robotics. The first reaction is that these assets are dumb: no revenue, no plan to monetize soon. But the author can understand it: historically breakthrough science came from research universities, government labs or Bell Labs, and now university funding is being cut and talent is being sucked into industry. AI is probably the first major technology in the past 50 years to emerge without government involvement, and in this era research is closed and secretive. So let Nvidia, with compute and cash in hand, plus a pile of VCs, fund these asymmetric bets. OpenAI and Anthropic are locked into the transformer paradigm and are unlikely to spend on researching these directions. The probability of failure is high, but most of the money is given in the form of compute anyway; if someone really strikes gold and forces the giants to pivot (say, to a more data-efficient architecture), the giants will most likely buy the discoverer at an eye-watering price, and one such deal pays for everything. The author thinks this is a better use of cash than continuing buybacks, and names Apple.

14:15 Tokens are burning, and nobody has measured ROI
Customers really are burning tokens, but are they getting ROI? The author asked across the ecosystem and the answer remains vague: don't know, nobody has measured it, it is all anecdote. He believes lower barriers to coding will hit knowledge work — financial firms used to hire a pile of reporting analysts to keep management on top of positions, and now two smart young analysts plus Claude writing a dashboard is enough, which he has seen with his own eyes. But for other AI capabilities, such as making spreadsheets and making presentations, the things marketing usually pushes, he has seen no obvious impact. Maybe it just needs more time, maybe it is a problem of intelligence itself. OpenAI recently published a blog on how agents accelerate internal research, but still frames AI's capability as intern level: it can execute routine tasks and is far from a real AI researcher. What he heard is that AI still lacks human research taste, though some believe sufficient scale can achieve it. And one thing holds for everyone in San Francisco: people are working harder than before. If the models are really that capable, why does everyone say they have more work? Maybe AI does not do our work for us but gives us more work.

15:17 Compute flips from shortage to glut in 2027
Everyone says shortage, shortage, two more years of shortage, and the author instead suspects things will not go as expected. His arithmetic is not complicated: usable AI data center capacity at the end of 2026 is estimated at about 15 gigawatts, with OpenAI and Anthropic each taking about 5 gigawatts; the supply chain will respond, and by the end of 2027 that number is estimated to hit 45-55 gigawatts, an increment of 30-40 gigawatts, of which the two giants take about 30 gigawatts. Assume half goes to training, leaving 15 gigawatts combined for inference. Inference is currently modeled at about $50 billion of revenue per gigawatt (a figure from Dylan Patel on Dashpod), and it can also be back-solved from Anthropic's deal to buy 300 megawatts from SpaceX for $1.25 billion a month; Dylan thinks smarter models can eventually push it to $100 billion per gigawatt. On that basis the two should produce $750 billion to $1.5 trillion of revenue in 2027. The author says that number is absurd: most people agree the two will do $150-200 billion this year, and next year he can barely imagine $400-500 billion, but $750 billion to $1.5 trillion is ‘two Walmarts’ or ‘two Toyotas’, a credibility stretch he does not think can be reached. He bets revenue per gigawatt is far below $100 billion or even $50 billion, possibly only a small fraction of it. The infrastructure side looks the same: assume 40 gigawatts lands in 2027, current rent is about $20 million per megawatt, implying a 3-year payback, so those 40 gigawatts would require $800 billion paid to infrastructure providers in 2027 alone. He does not think that can be collected either, which means rents have to fall and someone somewhere has to take a loss. Conclusion: in 2027 the supply chain will deliver a lot of compute, most of it in the second half, and he bets this pushes the market from shortage to glut. He stresses he is not saying the AI bubble will pop, only that we will soon be flooded with compute — 2026 is agentic demand meeting 2025 supply, supply will catch up and probably overshoot; but after that maybe the next stage of growth ignites and demand balloons again, for example persistent AI.

item.title: Stalin Was Just the Bookkeeper of the Revolution, and Then He Became General Secretary
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-empirehist-斯大林在革命里只是个管账的-后来却成了总书记/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-empirehist-斯大林在革命里只是个管账的-后来却成了总书记/
item.description: In 1917, while Lenin and Trotsky were on the streets calling for insurrection, Stalin was doing the organizing and fundraising nobody else wanted. He became General Secretary not by oratory but by sitting at the table.
item.content:encoded:
In 1917, while Lenin and Trotsky were on the streets calling for insurrection, Stalin was doing the organizing and fundraising nobody else wanted. He became General Secretary not by oratory but by sitting at the table.

This episode covers the groundwork before Stalin took power: Georgian origins, seminary, a failed bank robbery. Medium information density, but it makes clear why he was able to rise.

5:28 Even his birthday was something he changed himself
The parish register, the seminary certificate, the tsarist police file and his own handwritten questionnaire from the 1920s all say 18 December 1878. But the birthday he announced once in power was 21 December 1879 — a year and three days off. Bob Service offers one judgment in his biography: forgery was too easy for him. Service also has an unprovable but persuasive speculation — that changing his birthday helped him dodge conscription when he was young. The thing itself is the theme of the whole episode: this man's attitude toward facts was instrumental.

6:35 How anomalous it was for a Georgian to rule Moscow
His real name was Joseph Jugashvili, and he was born in Georgia. Georgia is in the Caucasus, next to Armenia, just north of Iran and Turkey, very far from Russia; it has its own language, its own alphabet, and its religion is Georgian Orthodoxy, which is not the same thing as Russian Orthodoxy. The analogy the episode gives is this: a man of Georgian Orthodox background climbing to the top of power in Moscow is equivalent to a man of Irish Catholic background from some remote place like Limerick becoming master of London in the mid-twentieth century. For Georgians at the time, being governed by Moscow meant being colonized.

8:43 His father refused to change trades, then started hitting people
His father Bessarion (nicknamed Besso) was a cobbler with his own workshop in Gori, and by most accounts a good craftsman. But he refused to keep up with the times: he went on making Georgian-style soft leather high boots while the market had already turned to European shoes. He did not adapt; he became bitter, drank heavily, and the violence fell mainly on his wife Ekaterina (Kiki) and little Joseph, who was nicknamed "Crazy Besso." Stalin later told his daughter Svetlana one scene: his father was drunk and beating his mother, he grabbed a knife and threw it at his father, missed, his father charged at him, and he ran to a neighbor's house and hid there for several days until his father's rage passed.

11:52 Smallpox, a carriage, and a left arm that was too short
Around age six he caught smallpox, severe enough that his mother thought he would die — two older brothers had already died in infancy, and the family was too poor to afford a doctor, so they could only call a local folk healer. He survived, but his face was permanently scarred, and every official photograph was retouched. Later a runaway carriage hit him and broke his arm; the left arm never healed properly and was noticeably shorter and stiffer for the rest of his life. The episode's formulation is: smallpox did not take him, his father's violence did not take him, and the carriage did not take him either. His mother was extremely devoted to him and had ambitious plans for him.

16:07 He wrote poetry, and he was good at it
In his late teens two things happened at once: he began writing quite good poetry, and he entered the seminary. The episode reads one poem aloud: "The pink buds have already blossomed, toward the pale violet violets; brushed by the breeze, the lily of the valley bends down over the grass. Flowers, my Georgia. May peace come to my native land, and may you, friends, make our homeland famous through study." Anita says that in the original Georgian it is quite beautiful. It shows two things: he was a proud Georgian, not a Russian; and in the tsarist context, this way of writing about a "homeland" was already close to sedition.

19:09 The seminary was the tsar's Russification machine
In 1894 he won a place at the Tbilisi seminary. The sign over the school said Georgian Orthodox, but in practice it was under the control of the Russian Orthodox Church, one of the institutions the tsar used to "Russify" the borderlands. Students were kept under close surveillance, and reports were written constantly: were these people good subjects of the tsar, were they talking sedition. And right under that surveillance, he was reading banned books, including What Is to Be Done? and other big questions about freedom and the individual. Anita's comment in the episode is: the surveillance here was not done well enough.

21:11 He gave himself the name of a bandit
On the banned list was a Georgian novel, Alexander Kazbegi's The Patricide, whose protagonist is a mountain fugitive named Koba. He took that name as his own alias, and at the seminary his classmates called him by it. The episode calls this a kind of "name determinism": he first took the name of a bandit hero, and then he really did become a bandit. The turning point from seminary student to bandit began when he saw with his own eyes two mountain bandits publicly hanged in the center of Gori for shooting a policeman over a stray cow — he was forbidden to watch, but he went.

24:16 They stole 250,000 rubles and could not spend a single one
In 1907 he and a group of friends ambushed a bank carriage in Yerevan Square in Tbilisi, almost within sight of the seminary: some stood up high and threw bombs down, others fired in the street, and the man who organized, financed and directed it from behind the scenes was Stalin, under the alias Koba. They got away with 250,000 rubles packed in linen sacks. But the bank had already published the serial numbers of its largest-denomination notes, so not one ruble of the money could be spent. It was the first time he left a police photograph on file, but he did not go to prison for it and essentially walked away untouched.

item.title: Outbound Reply Rate Near Zero? Don't Blame the Copy — Check Who You're Sending To First
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ycsp-外联回复率接近零-先别怪文案-先查你在发给谁/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ycsp-外联回复率接近零-先别怪文案-先查你在发给谁/
item.description: Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: get the person wrong and even perfect copy won't land. The YC partner's debugging order is — check the recipient first, then the company, then the subject line, and only then the copy.
item.content:encoded:
Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: get the person wrong and even perfect copy won't land. The YC partner's debugging order is — check the recipient first, then the company, then the subject line, and only then the copy.

Eight tactics in 12 minutes — dense, but every one is an action you can take immediately. For founders whose outbound reply rate is stuck in the single digits and who don't know what to change.

0:00 Send a hundred by hand before you talk about automation
The most common founder mistake is opening a tool, blasting a thousand emails, and getting zero replies. The real loss isn't the zero replies themselves — it's that you learned nothing from them. The problem could be the copy, the company targeting, the lead filtering, deliverability, or the subject line, and you can't tell which. So before automating, do at least a hundred outbound attempts by hand — genuinely by hand: spend time researching one specific person, what her problem is, what would grab her attention, read her LinkedIn and her company page. That homework is where high-converting outbound ideas come from.

1:04 Picking the right person matters far more than polishing copy
Founders often spend hours tweaking email wording while barely thinking about who they're sending to. Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: you have to find the person who has exactly the pain point you solve, or the most carefully polished copy won't land. One winter batch company selling infrastructure products should have been selling to senior engineering leaders, but its actual list was full of dev rel managers, GTM managers, and even customer success managers — it sent hundreds of emails and of course got no replies. Those wrong titles were never going to buy, regardless of how well the email was written.

2:06 Work backward from closed customers to the target title
How do you find the right title? Look at your existing customers first, then at the sales process: who pushed the last deal to close, who signed the contract, who paid the money — list all their titles and go find people with similar profiles. You can also look at who has replied to your outbound. If you're still at the very earliest stage, with neither customers nor replies, ask yourself: who in the organization benefits most from buying your software. Example: selling employee device security monitoring software, the chief security officer could get fired in a data breach, so he'll be interested; an engineering manager would probably rather not be monitored, so he's not a good target.

3:09 List-building tools will hand you the wrong companies
Another common mistake is searching in Sales Navigator and getting back a pile of results that look like a match but are the wrong type of company — search tech companies, for instance, and you often get a pile of IT implementation consultancies. So use list-building tools very carefully, and verify company by company whether it's really your customer. After doing enough outbound, you start spotting the clues that a company needs your product — intent signals. Job postings are a great thing to watch, since they reveal a company's priorities; company growth is another common signal: selling compensation planning software, companies under 100 people probably haven't introduced job levels yet, and companies over 500 have probably already set compensation bands, so crossing the 100-person mark is a great signal. Every product has signals like this; your job is to find your own.

4:09 Shake your first customers out of your personal network
When closing your first few customers, starting from your personal network is much easier and converts at a much higher rate. Really shake the tree — make sure you've covered everyone you know: first your personal network, then ask friends, family, investors, college roommates, people you met at a coffee shop for intros — literally anyone you can think of.

5:10 Executives don't care about your product features
The single most important thing in the email is clearly stating how you can help the other person. Figure out the three things that keep your buyer up at night: what could get him fired, what could get him promoted, and why he should believe you can help. When buyers read the email and think "this is exactly my problem," they're likely willing to take the call, even if they don't yet fully understand or trust your solution. The fact is executives don't care about your product features, don't care that your upload speed is blazing fast, and don't care that your database is written in rust — what they worry about is hitting the quarterly target. Keep the product description to one sentence at most, and save the details for the first call.

6:14 A good email reads like a peer wrote it, not like a pitch
The email of the founder of Aptin, a YC company from the S24 batch, is held up as an example: the tone is very casual, it sounds like a peer, it uses no jargon, it doesn't try to sound impressive, it reads like something a friend sent. He builds credibility with the first sentence — "I used to be a software engineer at Tesla. We got crazy good at using SMS to convert the people who visited our website into car buyers." The ending has a very clear call to action: would you be open to running an experiment to see whether AI can reactivate leads and lift conversion. The email also mentions that he noticed the phone number collected in the signup flow on their website, which makes it feel personalized; and the whole thing barely explains how the product works — it only talks about how to help the other person solve their problem.

8:20 On LinkedIn, mutual connections are the number one predictor
If email is about the subject line, LinkedIn is about your profile — it determines whether people accept your connection request and whether they reply. Key points: a photo boosts trust; turn the top banner into an ad for your company, stating clearly and concisely what the company does, avoiding jargon; rewrite the one-line headline and the about section into a short company description; move up what buyers care about (relevant and impressive experience, say) and cut what's irrelevant — if the about section is a pile of hobbies and interests, it's harder for buyers to see how you can help them. Another place worth investing in is mutual connections: the number of shared connections is the single biggest predictor of whether someone accepts a connection request, so accumulate relevant mutual connections with your target audience — it takes time, and you should turn it into a habit of using your full connection quota every day.

item.title: World Models Are Not Video Generation: Atlas Makes 3D Control an Input
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-a16z-世界模型不是视频生成-atlas-把-3d-控制做成了输入/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-a16z-世界模型不是视频生成-atlas-把-3d-控制做成了输入/
item.description: Language models process tokens; world models process physical space. Atlas's key move isn't generating longer video — it's putting the camera and reference images into 3D coordinates as inputs, turning generation from a slot machine into directing.
item.content:encoded:
Language models process tokens; world models process physical space. Atlas's key move isn't generating longer video — it's putting the camera and reference images into 3D coordinates as inputs, turning generation from a slot machine into directing.

23 minutes, medium information density, but Justin draws the line between world models and video generation very clearly. Worth hearing for anyone working in 3D, robotics, or VFX.

1:05 Atlas is a model release, not a product release
Justin clarifies right at the top: Atlas is not a product, it's World Labs' foundation model; products come later. It does three things — generate worlds that don't exist, reconstruct from real space, and simulate inside reconstructed space. Generation can start from text or an image, and then you can fly the camera straight through that world; reconstruction can take a single photo, or a hundred-plus, and the more photos the more accurate; simulation is aimed at VFX and robotics. That ordering itself says World Labs doesn't intend to ship a consumer app first — it wants to stand up a horizontal foundation model first, then let products grow on top of it.

4:09 Reference images are pinned into 3D space, not fed to the model
Video models tend to drift and hallucinate their own direction around the ten-second mark. Justin says Atlas's answer is spatial context: the reference images you give it aren't ordinary images — they're grounded in 3D space, so you can specify ‘put this one here, that one there’. When generating video you're not just giving a text prompt either; you're directly operating the camera, telling it to fly this way and that way, achieving precise pixel-level control. So even at a minute of generation, it's not pulling a slot machine — you are generating, directing, and controlling what the model outputs.

7:10 Atlas moves the 2D/3D fork earlier
Compared with Marble, World Labs' first product, Atlas is a completely rebuilt model stack. Marble put Gaussian splat at the center: video, 3D scenes, and meshes all had to pass through a Gaussian representation before being rendered back to image or video. Atlas breaks that dependency: the architecture is more unified and easier to scale, and the 2D/3D fork happens earlier. Generating 2D or video output is no longer bottlenecked on a Gaussian scene — the model emits 2D pixels directly; only in applications where you genuinely need 3D does it get lifted to 3D.

8:10 Gaussian isn't obsolete, it's just no longer mandatory
Justin doesn't think Gaussian has been outgrown — it's a tool, and you use it in the right place. VFX's final product is a 2D image or video, and may not need explicit 3D at all. But in real-time applications and on embedded devices, explicit 3D representations like Gaussian and mesh still have a place: in the future you might stream pixels in real time from a server farm, but we're not there yet, and it would be expensive, so for client-side rendering, mobile, and VR devices, Gaussian or mesh remains useful. Its other role is plugging into existing workflows — people in games, VFX, design, and architecture already have pipelines built on 3D representations, and rather than making them switch to fully AI-native all at once, it's better to bring AI into their workflow.

11:13 Simulation covers the last stretch of robot training
On the value of real to sim for robots, Justin says it's first of all evaluation: a robot ultimately has to work in a specific factory, with a specific machine, in a specific environment, and you have to make sure it works in exactly that environment. So simulation is useful in the last stretch of training and evaluation — build a simulation as close as possible to the final use case, then either fine-tune a pretrained robot foundation model directly in that simulation, or run evaluations to confirm it works. That gives you a path different from ‘collect a lot of demonstrations or teleoperate by hand’. He also describes a more aggressive version: take a few photos or casual videos with your phone, reconstruct the space with Atlas, describe the task in natural language, and let an agent build the simulation and do RL fine-tuning, yielding a robot adapted to that space within minutes.

14:16 OpenAI dropping world models may be an innovator's dilemma
The host asks why OpenAI turned that Sora direction — ‘video generation models are world simulators’ — into a consumer product back then, and now isn't doing world models. Justin says he won't comment on OpenAI's internal strategy, but offers one explanation: there may be an innovator's dilemma — you're holding something as strong as the LLM, and you're leading in that direction, so investing in the next thing isn't necessarily worth it. World Labs' judgment is that there's another class of model here, with a lot of opportunity, and they want to be the ones who seize it.

18:21 Three iPhones shooting bullet time came out far better than expected
Asked about hard physics, Justin says he hasn't tried a black hole and guesses it wouldn't be too impressive. What genuinely surprised him was bullet time: three iPhones on tripods doing synchronized capture, then using Atlas for a frozen-frame, orbit-around reframe. He cites the official example — a strawberry dropping into oat milk, time frozen at the instant the milk splashes up, flying a full circle around it, and the result is completely insane. This capability needs only three input viewpoints. That shows Atlas's value isn't only in ‘generating new worlds’ — it's also in turning a small amount of real footage into shots that traditionally required a large camera array.

19:21 3D is underrated on the input side
Justin says 3D has value in two places. On the output side people have already talked it to death — sometimes you just need explicit 3D assets to drop into a workflow or game engine. But 3D's value on the input side is underrated: even if the final output is a 2D VFX shot, giving the model a 3D control surface helps the director decide what kind of scene the model should output. You don't want to write ‘push in, pull out, move left’ in text — you want to grab the camera directly and have it zoom exactly the way you want, which text simply cannot describe. So Atlas makes camera control a native input type: one of the modalities in the multimodal mix is the camera.

item.title: Making a furin site isn't hard at all — admitting it isn't rare is
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-twiv-造一个-furin-位点根本不难-难的是承认它不罕见/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-twiv-造一个-furin-位点根本不难-难的是承认它不罕见/
item.description: Deep sequencing shows that a few genomes in every thousand of a coronavirus population carry insertions, and a furin site has been hit independently at the same position at least three times — the probabilistic argument for a lab origin doesn't hold up.
item.content:encoded:
Deep sequencing shows that a few genomes in every thousand of a coronavirus population carry insertions, and a furin site has been hit independently at the same position at least three times — the probabilistic argument for a lab origin doesn't hold up.

The first half is the quantitative methodology of viral recombination and insertion; the second half is the real target of this episode: dismantling the lab-origin argument with numbers. Listeners who want the argument can jump straight to 52 minutes.

6:07 They changed the GFP sequence and the recombination rate went up
The team first built an OC43 reverse-genetics system and made a pair of viruses: each carries a frameshifted GFP, so infection with either alone yields only fragments, but co-infection lets recombination stitch green fluorescent protein back together. They expected that changing the nucleotide sequence of one of the GFPs would lower the recombination rate; instead it rose. Paul says there is only a hypothesis for this, no data — one possibility is that once double-stranded RNA forms, the strand-transfer events of recombination become more likely because the duplex "breathes." This counterintuitive result later became the reagent starting point for the whole paper.

11:12 Knock GFP out of frame and let insertions reveal themselves
Measuring insertions and deletions is far harder than measuring point mutations, because they were thought to be rare and sequencing depth was insufficient. Their approach was to put the GFP gene into the viral genome and deliberately knock it out of frame, preceded by a start-codon peptide that is in a different frame from GFP, so the virus does not glow green; it turns green only when that site acquires an insertion or deletion of a particular length that pulls GFP back into frame. This lets them both count event frequencies and pick out green viruses to sequence and infer the mechanism. That is where figure 1 of the paper comes from.

13:15 Knocking out NSP15 made insertions go down
The original hypothesis came from prior work suggesting that NSP15, a nuclease, affects deletion rates — when you think nuclease, you naturally think deletions, not insertions. But the experiment went the opposite way: viruses with NSP15 showed a greatly increased rate of acquiring insertions that pulled GFP back into frame. Paul says the deletion rate numbers were not good enough this time to quantify, but the insertion result was black and white, and they were very surprised at the time — it was this accidental result that opened up the entire line of research.

22:26 Every base sequenced a million times before you talk about frequency
They moved from picking green viruses to brute-force sequencing: concentrating about 10 milliliters of virus down to 1 milliliter, loading a portion onto a sequencing chip, and producing hundreds of millions of reads, so that every nucleotide in the genome is read at least a million times, with roughly 30 human genomes' or 3 million viral genomes' worth of data per virus stock. Paul stresses that depth has to match the number of virions in the sample — sequencing hundreds of millions of times when the tube holds only a thousand virions is meaningless; they calibrated to sequence roughly a few percent of the viruses in the sample.

27:32 Eleven nucleotides is the threshold for judging origin
Short insertions (three to six nucleotides) can arise randomly in a viral genome, so their origin cannot be determined, and they were excluded from the analysis. They calculated that if an 11-nucleotide stretch matches the viral genome perfectly, the probability of that being pure chance is below 5%, so they restricted the analysis to insertions of 11 nucleotides or more. The result: over 90% matched the viral genome perfectly or nearly perfectly, and in OC43 wild-type virus had 87 times more insertions than the NSP15 mutant, most of them derived from the positive strand.

36:41 Insertions aren't rare events, they're a few per thousand
Vincent says that for years he was told insertions are rare, but the data suggest this has been happening all along. Paul responds that "rare" is a relative term: one in a million is rare, but if you have ten million of them, it's common. The insertion frequency they report is a few genomes per thousand — roughly five to ten genomes carrying an insertion out of every thousand virions. That frequency is lower than the point-mutation rate, but not by much. The reason it seemed rare in the past is that the vast majority of insertions are harmful or even lethal to the virus and get purged at low multiplicity of infection, so you cannot isolate them.

55:05 Making a furin site isn't hard at all
Mechanistically, a furin cleavage site needs at minimum two arginines, RXXR, and can even be cleaved with a single arginine plus other amino acids in support. Six of the 64 codons encode arginine, so multiplying the two fractions together, roughly 1% of random 12-base sequences will encode an RXR motif. There are about 30,000 different positions in a coronavirus genome where an insertion mutation can occur. So this is not some enormous engineering challenge.

57:08 Lightning strikes the same spot at least three times
Put the insertion frequency, the number of insertable sites, and the viral population size together, and the probability of a furin cleavage site appearing at one specific position in a coronavirus genome is not astonishing — and it roughly matches what deep sequencing actually measures. In their deep-sequencing data, which does not cover the whole population, they have already found new furin cleavage sites at least three independent times at the exact position of SARS-CoV-2's existing furin site. Paul says the numbers in the paper are an underestimate: they only focused on the spike region for PCR, and they required insertions to match the viral genome perfectly to rule out PCR artifacts, which very likely also excluded some naturally occurring sites that really exist.

item.title: Rome Won With a Crow: The Key to the First Punic War
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ancients-罗马的胜利靠一只乌鸦-第一次布匿战争的关键/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ancients-罗马的胜利靠一只乌鸦-第一次布匿战争的关键/
item.description: Rome turned sea battles into land battles with a boarding bridge called the corvus, cancelling Carthage's advantage in seamanship; but Carthage brought in a Spartan to rebuild its army and captured a Roman consul in return.
item.content:encoded:
Rome turned sea battles into land battles with a boarding bridge called the corvus, cancelling Carthage's advantage in seamanship; but Carthage brought in a Spartan to rebuild its army and captured a Roman consul in return.

This episode tells the First Punic War as a war story with mechanisms: the crow bridge, the sacred chickens, mercenaries, war elephants — all backed by concrete images and numbers, at high information density.

2:03 This was not a war between two equal powers
The host opens by calling this a clash of ‘the two great powers of the western Mediterranean,’ and Eve MacDonald corrects him on the spot: at the war's outbreak, Carthage was not necessarily a military power of that rank. Carthage had money, controlled the sea routes, and had centuries of alliance networks in western Sicily, but it had no strong standing army — it relied on allies and mercenaries. What actually made Carthage into a power capable of fighting Rome as an equal was this war itself. So the story Roman sources tell over and over, of ‘Roman adaptability,’ is only half the story; the other half is Carthaginian resilience and adaptability, without which there is no explaining why this war lasted more than twenty years.

15:29 Mercenaries at Messana dragged both powers into war
The trigger was not the ambition of Rome or Carthage but a group of Campanian mercenaries called the Mamertines. They had seized Messana, and after being defeated by Hiero II, king of Syracuse, they split in two: one faction asked Carthage for help, the other asked Rome. Carthage acted first from its base in the Lipari Islands, and Rome followed — and not with a small intervention, but a full invasion with two consular armies. Eve points out that the Roman sources' claim of an ‘accidental empire’ is highly suspect, because the Romans showed up at Messana at the scale of an invading force. Polybius treats the Romans' first crossing of the sea into Sicily as the starting point of Roman imperial expansion.

28:14 The corvus turned sea battles into land battles
Carthage was the naval power: better oarsmen, ships built fast and well — the Romans even built their warships to Carthaginian standards. But the Romans added one thing: the corvus, meaning ‘crow,’ a boarding bridge that could hook an enemy ship. Once hooked, the Carthaginian ship could not move, and Roman marines simply crossed over and fought a land battle. At the Battle of Mylae, the Carthaginians clearly did not expect this, and took heavy losses. Eve also cautions that the details of the corvus leave many unanswerable questions in the sources, but ancient historians all treat it as decisive. At the Battle of Cape Ecnomus, the corvus is again credited as the chief factor, and Rome thereby opened the sea route for its invasion of Africa.

38:40 Carthage hired a Spartan to rebuild its army
After the Roman landing in Africa, Rome advanced steadily and Carthage looked finished. Carthage's response was to recruit a new army in the eastern Mediterranean and to bring in a Spartan commander, Xanthippus. He reorganised the Carthaginian army and reworked how the war elephants were used. Eve notes in particular that the Carthaginians had not used war elephants before; it was only after seeing the Indian elephants Pyrrhus brought that they realised they had a smaller African elephant of their own they could use. Xanthippus's reforms worked: the Roman army was destroyed and the consul Regulus was captured. This was Rome's first devastating defeat of the war, and it became a key event in later Roman memory defining the relationship between Rome and Carthage.

43:11 The captured consul went back to Rome to argue against peace
Carthage sent the captured consul Regulus back to Rome to negotiate peace. In the Senate, Regulus said not to surrender, that Carthage was within reach. By agreement, if peace was not made, he had to return to Carthage and remain a prisoner. He went back, and died in captivity. Eve says the various horrifying versions of how he died are not actually mentioned in the credible sources, so it is hard to judge how much is later embellishment; but what is certain is that he died in captivity in Carthage, peace was refused, and Rome fought on. This passage is a textbook moment of Roman self-congratulatory rhetoric.

46:27 The sacred chickens would not eat, and Rome's fleet was finished
In 249 BC, the Roman consul Tiberius Claudius Pulcher took his fleet to fight Carthage off Drepana. By Roman ritual, the sacred chickens on his ship had to eat for the battle to proceed; if not, it was a bad omen. The chickens would not eat, so he threw them into the sea, saying that if they would not eat, then let them drink. Roman sources record this as the most serious act of sacrilege, and the Roman fleet was then defeated at Drepana. Eve says that once Roman sources start emphasising a commander's arrogance and contempt for tradition, it usually means something bad happened. This defeat kept Rome from sending out a fleet for eight years.

50:48 Hannibal's father held Rome down with guerrilla war
After Drepana, Rome vanished from the sea and Carthage gained freedom of action on the western coast. In 247 BC, Carthage sent a new commander, Hamilcar Barca — Hannibal's father.
