He brought a force Polybius calls the Mix-Hellenes, made up of soldiers of Greek, Libyan and Phoenician descent from North Africa, and waged guerrilla war against Rome, occupying the high ground above Drepana and Panormus, with considerable success. Eve says this was the first time in the war that Carthage's army fought Rome this well. He also seized the temple complex at Eryx, dedicated to the goddess the Carthaginians called Astarte, and both sides fought fiercely over this sacred site.

57:20 The rams from this war still lie on the seabed
The Battle of the Aegates Islands in 241 BC was the last battle. The Roman fleet hid behind the islands and ambushed a Carthaginian fleet heavy with supplies meant for Hamilcar. Eve says that if you climb Eryx today, on a clear day you can see the Aegates Islands perfectly, and Hamilcar very likely watched this disaster unfold from land. More remarkably, the site of this sea battle has been preserved underwater: over the past twenty years, underwater archaeologists have found large bronze rams on the seabed near the island of Levanzo, some inscribed with the names of Roman consuls, some bearing Punic inscriptions and carvings, along with Monte Fortino helmets and amphorae.

item.title: Bunsen Burners Don't Reduce Plate Contamination, and Vegetables Protect the Heart by Another Mechanism
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-thisweekinmicr-本生灯不减少平板污染-蔬菜护心另有机制/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-thisweekinmicr-本生灯不减少平板污染-蔬菜护心另有机制/
item.description: A Bunsen burner may actually increase settle colonies in low-contamination environments; the cardiovascular benefit of vegetables may not run through the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway but through gut bacteria turning nitrate and iron into DNIC that directly activates sGC.
item.content:encoded:
A Bunsen burner may actually increase settle colonies in low-contamination environments; the cardiovascular benefit of vegetables may not run through the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway but through gut bacteria turning nitrate and iron into DNIC that directly activates sGC.

The first half has a clean experimental design and a counterintuitive conclusion; the second half's DNIC paper has a complete mechanism but dense terminology, suited to those willing to chew through mechanism.

6:05 Bunsen burners don't reduce plate contamination
The authors used paired settle plates: one placed next to a lit Bunsen burner, one next to an unlit burner, both exposed simultaneously to the same contaminated airflow. The lit burner overall did not lower average contamination, and the statistical comparison showed no significant improvement. This directly challenges the common claim that there is a general sterile halo around the blue flame. The authors don't say the burner never helps, but that the effect depends on environmental conditions — they deliberately contaminated the lab air with Gordonia rubripertincta, then compared different flame sizes and dry versus wet particles.

10:13 83 CFU per minute is the crossover point
Under dry-particle conditions with an average 18 mm flame, they observed an apparent crossover point: when the airborne microbial concentration was above 83 CFU/minute, settle plates next to the burner tended to show less deposition; below that level, deposition tended to increase. This can explain decades of contradictory anecdotal experience: people in dry environments genuinely believe the burner helps, while people in modern air-conditioned labs with low airborne contamination genuinely find it useless or even worse. Relative humidity in a typical modern air-conditioned lab is usually between 40% and 60%.

13:43 Airflow isn't one-dimensional — don't light a burner in a laminar flow hood
The traditional view is that convection pulls contaminants upward, but the authors point out that the same airflow may first drag contaminated air laterally across the work surface before it rises. Any upward airflow must draw replacement air from somewhere, so the most important thing during aseptic work is to limit wind or airflow. This leads to the most practical point in the episode: there is no reason to light a Bunsen burner in a laminar flow hood, and the flame itself disrupts laminar flow. The authors did not directly visualize airflow; they measured a biologically relevant outcome — contamination — rather than fluid dynamics directly, and the authors themselves list this as a limitation.

17:49 Flaming tube mouths and lighting burners are both ritual
The authors draw a historical comparison with the old practice of flaming culture tube mouths. Michael's graduate advisor at the time said stop doing it, there's no evidence it helps, and produced the 1972 paper proving it. The judgment in the episode: changing behavior is hard, especially when a ritual gives people a sense of control — lighting the burner feels proactive, flaming the tube mouth feels like protecting the culture, but there's no evidence it actually does anything. The authors don't argue for abandoning the Bunsen burner; they argue for measuring: use simple settle plates to measure your own lab's environment and let evidence guide practice.

28:14 Vegetables may protect the heart via the DNIC pathway
This Cell paper proposes reframing the entire nitric oxide synthase pathway: not a local paracrine model (eNOS makes NO that acts on adjacent smooth muscle), but an endocrine-like circuit — nitric oxide synthase makes nitrate, nitrate enters the gut, is turned by microbes into dinitrosyl iron compounds (DNIC), which then act on targets such as the heart. If it holds up, the cardiovascular benefit of dietary nitrate (leafy greens, beets) may be mainly mediated by microbially generated DNIC, rather than the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway we currently believe in. The author is Andrei Kleshioff at the Karolinska Institute.

31:32 No DNIC found in germ-free mice
They used electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) to directly detect DNIC in tissues. Signals were visible in the liver and kidneys of healthy mice, but when the same detection was done in germ-free mice, no DNIC could be found in the tissue — the first hint that microbes are making it. After feeding inorganic nitrate, liver DNIC levels rose in conventional mice but not in germ-free mice; if ferric citrate was added to the nitrate drinking water, the liver DNIC signal rose even higher, while ferric citrate alone had no effect. The same in vitro: mouse and human feces plus nitrate plus iron can make DNIC, while germ-free mouse feces cannot.

39:55 DNIC directly activates sGC, not via free NO
They used isolated mouse aortic rings, pre-contracted with phenylephrine, then added DNIC. To distinguish free NO from direct sGC activation, they used two pharmacological tools: one that scavenges free NO, one that directly blocks sGC. The sGC blocker completely abolished DNIC-induced relaxation, while the free-NO scavenger only partially attenuated it. The conclusion is that DNIC activates sGC, but not through free NO — the FeNO2 entity itself appears to directly activate sGC. The same goes for bacterially generated DNIC: only wild-type E. coli supernatant (anaerobic, with nitrate and iron) relaxed aortic rings, while a mutant lacking nitrate reductase did not.

47:16 DNIC suppresses leucine uptake, holding down mTORC1
On the metabolic line, they measured the phosphorylation state of key proteins in the liver mTORC1 pathway. In disease-model mice, mTORC1 was overactivated, downstream S6K1 phosphorylation was elevated, and transcription factors driving lipid synthesis were also elevated. Both DNIC treatment and nitrate-plus-iron supplementation brought these markers back to control levels. Mechanistically, they used glioblastoma cells to measure radiolabeled leucine uptake and found that DNIC inhibits leucine uptake in a concentration-dependent manner, suggesting it inhibits the leucine transporter — leucine is the key signal telling mTORC1 that nutrients are available, so blocking uptake blocks mTORC1 activation.

item.title: Private credit's risk hides in insurance company ratings
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-excessreturns-私募信贷的风险藏在保险公司的评级里/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-excessreturns-私募信贷的风险藏在保险公司的评级里/
item.description: Private credit has poured into insurance companies, much of it in affiliated investments, rated by private agencies that are systematically too generous; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400-500 billion of capital a year.
item.content:encoded:
Private credit has poured into insurance companies, much of it in affiliated investments, rated by private agencies that are systematically too generous; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400-500 billion of capital a year.

The first half is industry lore; the real value is in the middle and back sections — the specific mechanics and numbers on private credit ratings, private equity in 401ks, and Social Security reform.

5:08 A stock fund should be 80-90% stocks
When Bob Posen took over as Fidelity's president in 1995, the firm was in an awkward spot: Jeff Vinick had moved half of the Magellan fund into cash, which both dragged on performance and violated holders' expectations of a stock fund. His approach was to build internal consensus first — if you run a stock fund, you must keep 80% to 90% of the position in the kind of stocks the fund's name implies; if you want balanced, if you want a money market fund, the firm has other products. His logic: investors bought this fund's stated positioning, and a manager cannot change that positioning just because he thinks "now is not a good time to buy stocks." That rule later became basic discipline for Fidelity's stock funds.

8:12 After doubling in size, keep the startup feel by splitting into small teams
Under Posen, Fidelity's assets under management grew from $500 billion to $1 trillion. His judgment was that the key to managing that much money is not process but how to preserve entrepreneurial spirit and a sense of belonging. The method was to split the investment team into relatively small groups — value, growth, small cap, international and so on — giving each group a stronger sense of ownership over results. At the same time he consolidated money market and bond funds in New Hampshire, because fixed income and money market funds look at the same credits, and here scale is a friend that spreads out enormous economies of scale; stock funds are exactly the opposite.

19:21 Put private equity in 401ks, but cap it at 10-20% first
Posen is reserved about putting private equity into 401ks. The core problem is liquidity: if a participant puts all their retirement assets into a single private equity fund, they simply cannot get the money out when hit by a medical emergency or when they reach the age for required minimum distributions. His proposal is that private equity should only be part of an asset-allocation fund or a target-date fund, not a standalone option; if it must be a standalone option, employers should set a cap, and the order of magnitude he gives is 10% to 20%. He draws an analogy to employer stock: GE employees who put their whole 401k into GE stock did not end well, and a retirement account needs diversification.

21:25 The instant markup in secondary trades is an accounting loophole
Private equity is hard to value to begin with, and what worries Posen most is secondary trades: a private fund, needing to raise cash or nearing the end of its investment period, sells part of its portfolio at a discount to another private fund. There is a technical loophole in the accounting rules that lets the buyer immediately mark that investment up to par on its books even though it bought at, say, a 5% discount. He believes this rule must be changed. Valuation is already hard enough; this "instant markup" should not be allowed to lift book value out of thin air and pass it through to holders via NAV.

24:28 Private ratings systematically overstate private credit
The private credit held by insurance companies, depending on how you count, can reach as much as $2 trillion, and a large share of it is "affiliated investments" — starting with Apollo, more and more private equity firms have become owners of insurance companies and then placed debt related to themselves into their own insurers. Posen and his co-authors found that a great deal of private credit is rated by private rating agencies, and that rating shopping exists. Two studies, from Columbia and Imperial College, show these private ratings are systematically too high; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400 billion to $500 billion of capital a year. His solution is direct: make the private ratings public and let the market pick apart the assumptions and methodology.

29:35 Mark Walter's $20 billion of affiliated credit is a wake-up call
Posen treats the Mark Walter case as a wake-up call. Walter founded Guggenheim and figured out early that buying a life insurer lets you steer what was a conservative insurance portfolio into higher-yielding securities, including private credit related to Guggenheim or to your own portfolio companies. The rules themselves allow insurers to invest in affiliated private credit, provided it is disclosed to regulators. Regulators have now found that insurers controlled by Walter or Guggenheim hold about $20 billion of affiliated private credit, some of which may have been used to buy the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Lakers. Walter's side is trying to divest part of the affiliated credit. Posen stresses this is not just Guggenheim: large private funds such as Apollo and KKR have all found insurance companies to be handy investment vehicles.

41:52 Someone with $1 million investable should not hold 40% bonds
Posen points out that most target-date funds arrive at retirement at 80% bonds and cash, 20% stocks, which is reasonable for people who must live off their retirement portfolio. But more than 7 million Americans have investable assets (excluding their primary residence) of over $1 million; they do not live off investment income and can ride out a down year in stocks. He calculates that over 30 years, a 60/40 portfolio and the 90/10 he advocates (90% stocks, 10% cash) differ by a factor of two in terminal value — the equivalent of $5 million versus $2.5 million. He rebuts the objections one by one: over the past 60 years bonds acted as a hedge in only 10 of them; in 2022 stocks and bonds both fell about 18%; stocks fall deeply, but look at two years, five years — after 2008, 2002 and 1974 they recovered and surpassed.

50:09 Semiannual reports are fine, but don't scrap first- and third-quarter filings
Posen supports keeping quarterly reporting and opposes moving to semiannual. The reason is that the economy, diplomacy and a company's own circumstances all change fast, and six months is a long time; moreover, the information vacuum created by semiannual reporting encourages insider trading. His compromise: full 10-Qs and 10-Ks at mid-year and year-end, and a slimmed-down report in the first and third quarters — three or four pages plus the income statement and balance sheet, not a heavy burden. He rebuts the claim that "less reporting encourages long-termism": when the UK made the move from quarterly to semiannual reporting optional in 2013-14, he and a quantitative accounting scholar at Columbia compared the two groups of companies, and the firms that switched to semiannual did not invest more in R&D or capital expenditure.

item.title: For thousands of years humans fought stench; perfume began as smoke burned for the gods
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-extracredits-人类几千年对抗恶臭-香水最初是烧给神的烟/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-extracredits-人类几千年对抗恶臭-香水最初是烧给神的烟/
item.description: Perfume did not start as luxury pleasure but as religious incense and disease prevention — Europeans believed foul air spread disease, so they wrapped themselves in scent.
item.content:encoded:
Perfume did not start as luxury pleasure but as religious incense and disease prevention — Europeans believed foul air spread disease, so they wrapped themselves in scent.

Medium information density, but it strings together perfume's religious origins, the plague and the decline of bathing, and the transformation of Grasse in France into one line — suited to anyone interested in the history of the senses and the history of consumption.

0:02 Ambergris comes from a battle inside a whale
The episode opens with a very concrete image to explain where ambergris comes from: a sperm whale swallows a giant squid, the squid's hard beak lodges in the whale's intestine, gets coated in a mysterious bile secretion and expelled, then drifts in ocean currents for decades before washing ashore. Apothecaries buy it at the price of gold by weight, grind it into a fixative, and use it to control how fast a scent evaporates, so the fragrance shifts slowly over a whole day. The image shows how absurdly long the raw-material chain of perfume can be — behind one scent lies a deep-sea struggle and decades of drifting on the currents.

2:04 Smell is the most emotional sense
The episode offers a judgment: by some measures smell is the most emotional sense, because it connects directly to the brain's memory center. Research shows that recalling a smell evokes memory more strongly than visualizing. Host Rob says his earliest memory is grabbing the rope seat of a lounge chair on Oahu's North Shore while learning to walk; what he remembers is not the image but the smell of that old rope fiber soaked in sea-salt wind. The other host's earliest olfactory memory is the old 80s formula of Trix cereal. Smell can offend, can give pleasure, can summon the past like a ghost, and is essentially untouchable, changeable, and evanescent.

3:04 The earliest perfume was smoke burned for the gods
Ancient perfume's origins were mainly religious, and it was not the distilled liquid of today — the earliest was basically smoke produced by burning. Egyptian priests burned specific woods, plants and resins to make pleasing smoke that both purified the ritual space and served as a channel connecting to the gods. The word perfume comes from the Latin perfumum, meaning "through smoke." In China, Southeast Asia and Native American communities alike, these fragrances were believed to be vehicles for communicating with deities, carrying prayers and pleas up to heaven or the spirit world. In Asia this developed into an incense-making tradition that largely replaced personal perfume until modern times, because the scent stayed in clothing and rooms.

7:07 Ibn Sina invented steam distillation
The 11th-century Arab scholar Ibn Sina discovered steam distillation: boiling a solid substance in water, collecting the steam, and separating the oil or essence from it. The first things extracted this way were rose water and rose oil, still a mainstay of cosmetic perfume today. Like many chemical, scientific and mathematical concepts, the method passed in the Middle Ages from Arab to European scholars, and then to Italy, which thereby became the center of European perfume-making throughout the Renaissance. The people making perfume then were often alchemists and apothecaries, and the perfumes they made were both drunk as medicine and worn on the body.

8:08 Scent was treated as an airborne barrier against disease
Before germ theory, European medical thought rested on miasma theory: foul or bad-smelling air was the main route by which disease spread. In an age without science this was not absurd, because rotting flesh, industrial burning and contaminated water really did make people sick. So Europeans concluded that inhaling sweet or pleasant air could ward off disease. The upper classes began using nosegays (a small bunch of dried flowers or herbs held up to the nose when passing foul smells), gentleman's canes topped with a container of aromatic substances, and perfumes worn, drunk or used to fumigate clothing as protection. Most famous is the plague doctor's mask, its hooked bird beak stuffed with flowers, spices and herbs.

9:08 The Black Death killed the public bathhouse
The Black Death may be the single biggest factor in Europe's adoption of perfume. The plague that swept Europe for three centuries killed off the public bathhouses left over from the Roman Empire, because people believed water was a vehicle of infection. Moral norms then shifted, religious concern about public nudity grew, and bathhouses came to be seen as places of assignation or sex work. People switched to cleaning their hands and faces with damp cloths, and soaking baths became increasingly rare. They began wearing more underclothes to absorb sweat and odor so the garments could be changed and washed. In this environment, not only the upper class but the rising middle class relied more on perfume, often making it at home from rosemary in the garden or alcohol plus purchased ingredients.

10:09 Perfumed gloves set off a political scandal
In the 16th century people usually scented their clothes rather than their bodies, and perfumed gloves, handkerchiefs and fans were especially popular. The French queen Catherine de Medici brought Italian perfumery traditions to the French court and hired the Italian perfumer Renato Bianco (Master Rene) to blend exclusive scents for her. Legend has it that Master Rene had a secret tunnel connecting his residence to Catherine's bedroom, and that he also served as her poisoner. When Catherine's rival Jeanne III of Navarre died after receiving a pair of perfumed gloves as a gift from Catherine, rumors spread that the gloves had been soaked in poison. Whether the poisoned gloves were real or not, several deaths were allegedly attributed to them, to the point that William Cecil advised the perfume-loving Elizabeth I to refuse any gift of scented clothing.

12:09 Grasse shifted from leather tanning to perfume
Catherine de Medici's passion for perfume changed the industry forever. The French city of Grasse realized the flower fields around it made it an ideal place for fragrance manufacturing, and with Catherine's support shifted its economic base from leather tanning to perfume-making; the city, and the country as a whole, remains the center of world perfume manufacturing to this day. France began to dominate the spice and fragrance trade, and the French empire could bring in novel, distant raw materials from the Caribbean, Indonesia, India and China. French perfumers also created the language we use to describe perfume, and the three stages of a scent's evolution: top notes or head notes smelled in the first few minutes, middle notes that can last for hours, and base notes smelled in the evening or the next day. This evolution comes from fixatives controlling evaporation speed, such as ambergris or alcohol, revealing layers of fragrance over time.

item.title: Astra Crosses the AGI Threshold, but No One Can Audit It
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-cogrev-astra-跨过-agi-门槛-但没人能审计它/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-cogrev-astra-跨过-agi-门槛-但没人能审计它/
item.description: Astra frees humans from ever having to do certain tasks again, yet OpenAI paused only half its RL compute; external audits get stuck two or three days before release, and there is no adult in the room to take the blame.
item.content:encoded:
Astra frees humans from ever having to do certain tasks again, yet OpenAI paused only half its RL compute; external audits get stuck two or three days before release, and there is no adult in the room to take the blame.

The two hosts chain together the evidence for Astra's capabilities, the true magnitude of OpenAI's pause announcement, why auditing can't get off the ground, and why doomers can't hedge by shorting — high information density.

3:30 Astra holds long tasks together with a single notes file
In the past, models handling long tasks compressed a million tokens into a summary and opened a new window, losing all the detail. Astra instead maintains a long-lived notes file that the model updates at any time and carries forward with it, no matter how many tokens have already been written, and it can also search back through its own session history. So the same million-token context window can effectively manage roughly ten times that much context within a single rollout. Nathan calls this a mechanism that is "obvious in hindsight but genuinely new."

6:19 OpenAI self-reports 3.1 agent workdays per workday
In its research-acceleration blog post, OpenAI gives its own unit of measure, the "agent workday," reporting that each human workday corresponds to 3.1 agent workdays. Nathan admits the methodology is unclear; his reading is the literal one: for every eight-hour shift a human researcher puts in, the agent runs twenty-four hours in real time. The same post also has a chart grouping by human time spent and looking at Astra's success rate, effectively a substitute for the METR curve. Nathan says the METR curve hasn't been updated in a long time — not for lack of wanting to, but because the tasks aren't big enough anymore: the model iteration cycle is now shorter than the task length that needs to be measured.

21:03 External audits are structurally stuck at two or three days
Prakash breaks down why external auditing can't get off the ground: there are a hundred candidates in a model's lifecycle, and the release version is only settled in the final two or three days, so external auditors get only a few days. Bringing the audit team into the company a month early runs into a second layer of problems — audit firms are short on people and money, depend on funding from model companies, and their staff keep flowing to model companies; and if two companies agreed not to poach from audit firms, that would itself be an antitrust problem. He says the revolving-door problem in financial regulation remains unsolved to this day.

31:12 What was announced as a pause was only half a pause
Nathan reads OpenAI's RL compute chart: what was announced was a "frontier scale RL pause," but in reality, when the Hugging Face incident was disclosed, half was paused first and the other half kept running — and that half was already enough for the Astra model to take over part of OpenAI's research infrastructure; even so it wasn't fully stopped, only half was cut. As for whether the remaining blue category labeled "non Astra" contains a model stronger than Astra, he says he doesn't know, but "I've been disappointed before." Prakash adds: the real frontier model isn't the deployed one, nor the one being trained, but the one in the researcher's head, because those ideas become models twelve to eighteen months later.

39:05 There is no adult in the room to take the blame
Prakash's rebuttal to Jacob Coxen's line that "accepting this race and entering the endgame is an arrogant gamble launched from a private company's Slack" is: then who do you want to hand it to? Pete Hegseth's Signal group? His judgment is that there is "no adult in the room" — no external savior, the whole world is held together with duct tape, and most of the smartest, most capable people to handle this are already inside these companies. Hand the decision to the government and what you get is political legitimacy, not wisdom, nor the legitimacy needed for execution. So the starting point has to be accepting that the world is just like this.

46:03 Operation Warp Speed is the precedent for a safe harbor
Nathan proposes the government should set a hard deadline the way you would with a child: you sort it out yourselves, here's the deadline, and if you can't, I come in and play the bad guy. The accompanying move is to first remove the antitrust excuse. Prakash counters with Operation Warp Speed: the pharma companies specifically demanded an exemption from vaccine liability claims, wanted a safe harbor, and actually got legislation; without that exemption, they would have been sued into bankruptcy after the pandemic. So lawyers warning that "there will be retroactive reckoning in the future" is not alarmism — even if all current decision-makers agree, it doesn't matter, because the only thing that binds future decision-makers is law, not the verbal promises of today's people.

1:00:40 FSD's mistake is putting a human in the loop
Raffi has crashed a Tesla using FSD. His judgment is that FSD's interface design is bad, because it claims a human in the loop but when it actually hands control to the user it doesn't give enough time to understand the situation and decide what to do; Waymo's design premise is that there is no human to take over, so the safety argument is completely different. He personally would be willing to drive FSD again on the highway, or at least sit behind the wheel, but would be more hesitant on local streets in Palo Alto. The same company also has two kinds of code contracts: the Firefox team only allows humans to commit, while the Mozilla AI team has an entire codebase not a single line of which was written by a human — people only write the spec, and the whole codebase is automatically regenerated when CI builds.

1:29:15 The takeover is already complete, no one just admits it
The key disagreement between Prakash and Daniel: Daniel hasn't realized this has already happened. The financial market itself is the paper clipper, the means of production is the financial market, and the financial market is already fully fused with AI. Humanity took about a hundred years to hand complete control of the means of production to the financial market. He says don't think of AI as a chat box; it's a global information process that doesn't have to run in a single box, and doesn't even have to be silicon-based — humans together with AI agents can constitute this information process. The reason Jacob became disillusioned is that he discovered in the Slack group that there was no control at all, yet he still assumed there existed somewhere in the world a group that could actually make decisions.
